item.title: Raji community fears for survival of its endangered language
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: Children in the Raji community not only struggle to speak their mother tongue, Raji, but also face difficulty in understanding their elders. item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: Children in the Raji community not only struggle to speak their mother tongue, Raji, but also face difficulty in understanding their elders. With declining usage among the younger generation and an absence from school curricula, the Raji language is facing a crisis of generational shift.

​Man Bahadur Raji of Bheriganga Municipality-12, Surkhet, always tries to speak Raji with his children and grandchildren. However, they barely comprehend a few words. The language, rarely heard inside the home, has become alien to them.

​”When we were young, everything at home, in the forests, and during gatherings was spoken in Raji,” he said. “Now, the number of speakers is declining. I fear the language will die with us.”

Although community-led language classes were run for the younger generation, he said the initiative did not achieve much success.

The local community ran language classes with the support of the Bheriganga Municipality in the last fiscal year. But children reverted to speaking Nepali outside the classroom. A lack of practice at home and in the community prevented the native tongue from taking root.

​Man Bahadur’s concern is linked to the identity of the entire community. The endangered Raji indigenous group’s mother tongue is now facing an existential struggle. Despite the implementation of federalism aimed at linking local languages, culture, and knowledge with school education, Raji has not been able to find a place in local curricula. Under federalism, local governments have the authority to incorporate regional language, culture, history, skills and traditions into education to preserve local identity. However, for the Raji community in Karnali Province, this opportunity has yet to be realized.

​Recognized by the government as an endangered indigenous group, the Raji people possess a distinct language, attire, rituals and culture. However, they lack a written script.

According to the 2021 census, the Raji population stands at 5,125-2,483 males and 2,642 females. Nearly half of the population resides in Kailali, while Surkhet and Bardiya account for roughly 21% and 11%, respectively.

​Ganga Bahadur Raji, also from Bheriganga-12, attributed the decline primarily to fading usage among the young. “Children only speak Nepali now. How can it survive if it isn’t spoken at home?” he asked. “Local government initiatives also lack effective, long-term strategies.

Ganga Bahadur believes that including Raji language and culture in the local curriculum would enable children to learn about their community’s history, language and identity.

“Once the language is taught in schools, children will learn it, and once they learn it, the language can gradually survive,” he said. “At present, the responsibility of preserving the language rests solely on the shoulders of the elderly, and that is not enough.”

​According to the 2021 census, the Raji population stands at 5,125-2,483 males and 2,642 females. Nearly half of the population resides in Kailali, while Surkhet and Bardiya account for roughly 21% and 11%, respectively. The Raji population is divided into three clans: Naukalya, Bahrabandali, and Sutur Pande. ​All share the same mother tongue, a Tibeto-Burman language in the Raji-Raute group of the Sino-Tibetan family.

The 2021 census recorded 4,876 Raji speakers—representing 82.1% of the ethnic population. The Raji people are historically nomadic. Although they have transitioned to settled life, their linguistic footprint is shrinking gradually.

Realizing that intercaste marriages have posed serious challenges to the preservation of the Raji language and culture, the community has been making efforts to organize marriages within the community, as well as the preservation of their language, traditional attire and cultural practices. Although they have also been conducting awareness campaigns and cultural preservation activities through the Raji Salm Society, these efforts have not been sufficient, according to Ashok Raji, general secretary of the Raji Salm Society.

The international linguistic organization, Ethnologue, has listed Raji as an “endangered” language due to weak intergenerational transmission and absence from school instruction.

​A decade-old study in a Raji settlement in Thauri of Surkhet found that out of 45 people across 12 households, only 18 individuals—all over age 40—could speak Raji fluently. The study found that although the younger generation understood a few words, they were found to be unable to speak the language.

“Only our surnames remain Raji; we have lost everything else,” lamented Birkha Lal Raji, a member of the Raji community.

Man Bahadur Raji, who can still sing traditional songs and recount folklore in his mother tongue, fears the language will die by the time of his grandchildren. “We are old now. Who will speak the language after us?” he asked.

​Absence from Local Curricula

​Although local governments have designed customized curricula under the federal system, even local governments with a substantial Raji population have not included the language in their local curricula. Birendranagar Municipality has prepared a local curriculum, but it has nothing related to the Raji language.

“We organize one or two programs for the Raji community every fiscal year, but nothing has been done yet to include the community’s language in the local curricula,” said Tanka Prakash Lamichhane, the information officer for Birendranagar Municipality.

Bheriganga Municipality has prepared local curricula for Grades 1 through 5. But here also the curricula lack dedicated chapters for the conservation and study of Raji language.

Gajendra Kumar GC, head of the Education, Youth, and Sports branch at the municipality, said they were facing difficulty due to the community’s small population. “Including only the Raji language in the curriculum might lead to demands from other communities,” he said. “Although there is some information about the community, there are no dedicated chapters for the Raji language. Maybe we can add something while revising the curricula.”

​Ashok Raji of Raji Salm Society criticized all levels of government for failing to conduct comprehensive studies on the community’s realities.

“The Raji community is one of the marginalized and minority indigenous groups. There is not enough content about our language and community in the local curriculum. This is a result of the failure to reach the community and of the way our community is perceived,” he said. “Merely holding basic interactions won’t save a language.”

He demanded targeted budget allocations for dictionaries, teaching materials and school programs.

​Although the Language Commission has prepared a Raji grammar reference book, practical implementation remains non-existent. “The grammar exists in books, but not in schools,” Ashok Raji said. “If children cannot read it, how will the language survive?”

Man Bahadur Raji, who can still sing traditional songs and recount folklore in his mother tongue, fears the language will die by the time of his grandchildren.

“We are old now. Who will speak the language after us?” he asked.

item.title: LPG shortage hits small businesses, consumers in Karnali
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: A growing shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) has severely affected small hotels and restaurants across Karnali province. The shortage has forced several businesses to close and pushed others to rely on firewood and electric stoves. Local business owners in Surkhet and nine surrounding districts—Dailekh, Kalikot, Jumla, Mugu, Humla, Dolpa, Jajarkot, Salyan and Rukum […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: A growing shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) has severely affected small hotels and restaurants across Karnali province. The shortage has forced several businesses to close and pushed others to rely on firewood and electric stoves.

Local business owners in Surkhet and nine surrounding districts—Dailekh, Kalikot, Jumla, Mugu, Humla, Dolpa, Jajarkot, Salyan and Rukum West—say cooking gas is no longer available in the market.

Household consumers as well as small-scale commercial ventures, including eateries and bakeries, have been affected as the current supply is far lower than the demand.

While larger hotels and restaurants are somehow continuing operations by transporting LPG cylinders from as far as Nepalgunj, smaller operators say importing gas from outside the district is financially unsustainable for them. This has left them with little choice but to suspend operations.

Jagat Panta, a local LPG distributor, said more than 500 customers queued on Monday for a shipment of just 150 cylinders. Even when distributing gas under local administrative supervision, more than 300 customers were turned away empty-handed after waiting for hours. Distributors say while they are continuing to collect empty cylinders from consumers, they cannot secure enough refilled cylinders from suppliers to meet the growing demand.

Business owners say alternative cooking methods cannot be of much help for them due to unreliable electricity grids in the region.

The District Administration Office, Surkhet, has directed distributors to reserve 10% of incoming gas supplies for vulnerable groups and students. Assistant Chief District Officer Dil Bahadur Karki said the lack of a dedicated gas depot in Surkhet has worsened the supply challenge in the district.

The local administration has introduced a pass system to distribute gas to people with disabilities, new mothers, elderly citizens and students. A total of 116 cylinders were distributed to these targeted groups on Monday and Tuesday.

Local authorities have increased market monitoring and dispatched police personnel to oversee distribution points to prevent hoarding.

According to Nepal Oil Corporation, 41,517 filled cylinders were delivered to Surkhet between August 1 and August 8.

The deceased has been identified as Phalato Shahi—the mother of Prakash Shahi, one of the community’s chieftains. According to Lal Bahadur KC, an employee with a project […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: The total population of the endangered Raute community, which continues to live a nomadic forest-based lifestyle, has dropped to 132 with the death of a 65-year-old woman.

The deceased has been identified as Phalato Shahi—the mother of Prakash Shahi, one of the community’s chieftains.

According to Lal Bahadur KC, an employee with a project working for the well-being of the community, Shahi had been suffering from a chronic illness and was undergoing medical treatment. “She was under medication,” KC said. “Members of the community also consumed excessive alcohol during the recent Saune Sankranti festival. She died at around 2 am on Thursday.”

The community’s population stood at 135 in Shrawan (mid-July to mid-August) last year.

The community shifts its settlement depending on the availability of forest resources. It is currently living in Khanikhola of Simta Rural Municipality-9 in eastern Surkhet.

item.title: Jajarkot finds its footing again two years after the quake
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: A devastating earthquake that struck late on November 3, 2023, changed the lives of thousands of families in Bheri Municipality, Nalgad Municipality and Barekot Rural Municipality of Jajarkot in a matter of moments. Hundreds lost their loved ones. Homes collapsed, irrigation canals were damaged, water mills stopped operating, marketplaces fell silent, and many families […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: A devastating earthquake that struck late on November 3, 2023, changed the lives of thousands of families in Bheri Municipality, Nalgad Municipality and Barekot Rural Municipality of Jajarkot in a matter of moments.

Hundreds lost their loved ones. Homes collapsed, irrigation canals were damaged, water mills stopped operating, marketplaces fell silent, and many families were forced to live in temporary shelters. For two years, many farmers were unable to continue regular farm work. As a result, agricultural production declined, incomes dried up and uncertainty about the future deepened.

Today, greenery is gradually returning to those quake-affected settlements. Irrigation canals have been restored, locals are busy with farm work, water mills are running again, and local markets are thriving. Locals say reconstruction has begun to restore confidence and hope for self-reliance in the community.

The “Livelihood Improvement and Disaster Resilience Enhancement Program” has been launched with financial support from the Government of Japan, in partnership with UNDP and UN-Habitat, to support recovery and improve livelihoods. The program is implemented by Chhaya Nepal.

Shared service centers, marketplaces, irrigation canals, water ponds and other community infrastructure have been built and restored under the program. Likewise, various capacity-building and income-generating initiatives have been implemented in the quake-hit areas.

Irrigation system restored after two years

For Kamala Oli of Ranikhet in Nalgad-5, the earthquake brought not only the loss of shelter but also concern over food. “We depended on farming for our livelihood. The earthquake severely damaged the land I was cultivating,” she said.

With irrigation canals destroyed, her fields lacked water, making it impossible to grow crops for two years. As a result, vegetable and paddy production was disrupted, which directly affected her family’s income and livelihood.

“Earlier, it was extremely difficult to continue farm activities without water,” she said. “Now that the canal has been rebuilt, both vegetables and crops are growing well. The water mill is operating again. Income has increased, and hope for the future has returned.”

Many farmers like Kamala say rebuilt irrigation canals have helped revive agricultural activity in the village.

Income rises with farming

According to Prashant Oli of Chhepka in Nalgad-2, damage to irrigation canals deprived 122 households of adequate irrigation for two years. This forced local farmers to rely only on seasonal crops during the monsoon.

“Now that the canal has been repaired, farming can be done year-round,” he said. “Vegetable production has increased, and it is easier to sell in the market. Our incomes are gradually improving.”

Locals say many farmers have now begun commercial vegetable farming.

Min Rawal, Karnali Province manager of Chhaya Nepal, said the program aims not only to rebuild damaged structures but also to make communities economically and socially self-reliant. He said programs such as irrigation, livelihood support, capacity building and community infrastructure development have been implemented in an integrated manner.

“Our priority is to strengthen the ability of the local community to recover after disasters,” Rawal said. “By expanding income opportunities alongside infrastructure development, we are aiming to build long-term resilience.”

Bir Bahadur Giri, chairperson of Barekot Rural Municipality, said agricultural production has increased alongside reconstruction.

“Earlier, there was despair in the village. Now farmers have increased production, market transactions have grown and confidence has returned to the community,” he said.

Bheri Municipality Mayor Chandra Prakash Gharti also said reconstruction has brought new energy to affected communities.

“The cooperation among local governments, development partners and communities has laid the foundation for sustainable rebuilding,” he said. “The earthquake caused immense damage, but reconstruction has given communities the strength to move forward again.”

Shared service centers, marketplaces, irrigation canals, ponds and other infrastructure built in Bheri, Nalgad and Barekot are now helping to expand local economic activity. Increased agricultural production and improved market access have played a significant role in restoring livelihoods after the disaster, locals say.

The earthquake destroyed homes, shattered dreams and forced many families into hardship. But reconstruction efforts have opened pathways to new hope, new opportunities and self-reliance. As homes and infrastructure rise again, so does community confidence.

item.title: Road accidents surge 23% in Karnali
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: The number of road accidents in Karnali Province increased by 23% in the fiscal year 2025/26 compared to the previous year. The death toll, however, fell by three percent, according to the Nepal Police Highway Safety and Traffic Management Office in Birendranagar. According to the office’s annual report, a total of 1,197 road accidents […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: The number of road accidents in Karnali Province increased by 23% in the fiscal year 2025/26 compared to the previous year.

The death toll, however, fell by three percent, according to the Nepal Police Highway Safety and Traffic Management Office in Birendranagar.

According to the office’s annual report, a total of 1,197 road accidents were recorded across the province during the year. The accidents claimed 135 lives and left 2,307 people injured.

SP Mukunda Prasad Rijal, chief of the office, said overspeeding was the leading cause of accidents during the review year.

Of the total crashes, 671, or 62%, were attributed to speeding. Other causes included 112 accidents due to miscellaneous reasons, 51 caused by driver incompetence, 48 linked to drink-driving, 39 involving pedestrians, 20 while overtaking, 18 due to mechanical failure and eight caused by brake failure. A small number of accidents resulted from adverse weather conditions.

Motorcycles accounted for 738 vehicles involved in crashes, representing about 47% of the total, according to the report. Jeeps, cars and vans accounted for 17% of the crashes, followed by auto-rickshaws and tempos (14%), tractors (7%), microbuses (6%), trucks and tankers (4%), and buses (3%).

By age group, people between 26 and 40 years accounted for the highest number of accidents. This represented 44% of the total. According to the office, people in this age bracket travel the most, drive more frequently, and are more active on the roads for employment. This increases their risk of being involved in crashes, it added.

Likewise, the highest number of accidents, 43%, occurred between noon and 6 pm.

District-wise, Surkhet was the most accident-prone district. Of the 1,197 accidents recorded across the province, 690 occurred in Surkhet alone. Rukum West was next with 139 accidents, followed by Dailekh (85), Salyan (75), Jajarkot (56), Jumla (46), Kalikot (42), Dolpa (28), Humla (19) and Mugu (17).

According to the office, the rise in accidents is mainly due to the rapid increase in the number of vehicles, narrow and deteriorating local roads, a shortage of traffic police personnel, inadequate road safety infrastructure and technically unfit vehicles.

Vehicle registrations in the province increased by 16.27% in fiscal year 2025/26.

Meanwhile, cases of traffic rule violations declined during the year. According to the office, traffic enforcement actions fell by 23% from the previous fiscal year to 29,775 cases. Revenue collected from fines also dropped by 20% to Rs 27.22 million.

item.title: No-confidence motion registered against Karnali Chief Minister Kandel
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: Opposition lawmakers have registered a no-confidence motion against Karnali Chief Minister Yamlal Kandel. Lawmakers from the Nepali Congress (NC) and the Nepal Communist Party (NCP) registered the motion on Thursday. A total of 16 lawmakers, five from the NC and 11 from the NCP, have proposed NC parliamentary party leader Jeevan Bahadur Shahi as […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: Opposition lawmakers have registered a no-confidence motion against Karnali Chief Minister Yamlal Kandel.

Lawmakers from the Nepali Congress (NC) and the Nepal Communist Party (NCP) registered the motion on Thursday.

A total of 16 lawmakers, five from the NC and 11 from the NCP, have proposed NC parliamentary party leader Jeevan Bahadur Shahi as the province’s new Chief Minister. Although the NC has 14 lawmakers in the Karnali Provincial Assembly, only five have signed the no-confidence motion.

According to NCP Chief Whip Krishna Bahadur BC, the no-confidence motion was registered as part of efforts to form a new ruling coalition.

The move comes a day after Nepali Congress (NC) ministers withdrew from the UML-led provincial government.

A support of 21 lawmakers is required to form a government in the 40-member Karnali Provincial Assembly. NC and NCP have 14 members each in the provincial assembly, while UML has 10 and RPP has one lawmaker. The provincial assembly also has one independent lawmaker.

item.dc:creator: bishnu

The four ministers submitted their collective resignations to Chief Minister Yamlal Kandel before the provincial cabinet meeting on Wednesday morning. Former Minister for Social Development Ghanashyam Bhandari confirmed the resignations. “Yes, […]
item.content:encoded:
KATHMANDU: The Karnali Provincial Government has fallen into uncertainty after all four ministers from the Nepali Congress (NC) tendered their resignations on Wednesday morning.

The four ministers submitted their collective resignations to Chief Minister Yamlal Kandel before the provincial cabinet meeting on Wednesday morning.

Former Minister for Social Development Ghanashyam Bhandari confirmed the resignations. “Yes, all four of us have resigned,” Bhandari told Himal Press.

NC had four ministers in the provincial government: Ghanshyam Bhandari, Rajiv Bikram Shah, Suresh Adhikari and Bijaya Budha.

Kandel was appointed chief minister on April 9, 2024, with the support of the then CPN (Maoist Center). After the Maoist Center-led federal government collapsed, the NC and CPN-UML formed a coalition at both the federal and provincial levels. Under that alliance, four NC ministers joined Kandel’s government under parliamentary party leader Shah’s leadership on August 4, 2024.

The seven-member Karnali cabinet consisted of four ministers from the NC and three from the CPN-UML.

NC leaders say the party decided to step down after Chief Minister Kandel did not honor an understanding under which the NC and the UML had agreed to lead the provincial government in turn.

The 40-member Karnali Provincial Assembly requires 21 votes for a majority. NC and the Nepali Communist Party (NCP) have 14 seats each, while UML has 10 seats and the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) has one. One is an independent lawmaker.

Kandal cannot command a majority in the provincial assembly without the support of either the NC or the NCP.

item.title: Dolpa jeep accident leaves one dead, 13 injured
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: One person has died and 13 others were injured when a jeep met with an accident in Maurelekh in Ward-4 of Jagdulla Rural Municipality of Dolpa on Sunday afternoon. According to police, the jeep heading to Jumla from Majhgaon in Jagdulla–4 went out of control and fell some 20–25 meters off the road. A […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: One person has died and 13 others were injured when a jeep met with an accident in Maurelekh in Ward-4 of Jagdulla Rural Municipality of Dolpa on Sunday afternoon.

According to police, the jeep heading to Jumla from Majhgaon in Jagdulla–4 went out of control and fell some 20–25 meters off the road.

A total of 14, including the driver, were on board the jeep. The deceased has been identified as Bishnu Thapa (38) of Tripurasundari Municipality–8 in Dolpa. The remaining 13 were injured in the incident.

Efforts are underway to rescue the injured and transport them to Jumla for treatment.

item.title: Use choppers if needed for search operation: Chief Minister Kandel
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: Karnali Chief Minister Yam Lal Kadel has directed authorities to deploy helicopters, if necessary, for the search of passengers of a minibus that plunged into the Karnali River on Thursday morning. During discussions with provincial chiefs of the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, the Armed Police Force and the National Investigation Department on Friday, Kandel […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: Karnali Chief Minister Yam Lal Kadel has directed authorities to deploy helicopters, if necessary, for the search of passengers of a minibus that plunged into the Karnali River on Thursday morning.

During discussions with provincial chiefs of the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, the Armed Police Force and the National Investigation Department on Friday, Kandel urged them to intensify the search operation by mobilizing all available resources. While appreciating the efforts made so far by security agencies, Kandel said helicopters should also be used if required.

He also instructed officials to expand the search area from Dailekh to the Indian border, from where Karnali enters India.

During the meeting, Armed Police Force (APF) DIG Krishna Raj Pathak said divers had already been deployed at the incident site. He added that additional divers from Kurintar of Chitwan are also joining the rescue team.

Similarly, Nepal Police DIG Jayaraj Sapkota briefed the Chief Minister that muddy water, strong currents and difficult terrain were creating challenges to the search operation. He added that all security agencies were jointly mobilizing available manpower and resources to continue the search.
The Nepali Army personnel has also been deployed for the search operation. Drone cameras have also been deployed to scan possible locations.

The minibus heading to Kalikot from Surkhet veered off the Karnali Highway at Chamunda Bindrasaini of Daielkh and fell some 400 meters into the Karnali River on Thursday morning. A body was recovered from the cliff, while the vehicle and the remaining passengers are still missing.

item.title: Exclusive breastfeeding rates improving in Karnali
item.dc:creator: bishnu
item.description: SURKHET: While the rate of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months has been steadily declining in Nepal in recent years, breastfeeding rates are improving in Karnali Province. Karnali is now among the country’s top-performing provinces on this indicator. According to the Nepal Demographic and Health Survey, 74% of infants in Karnali are exclusively breastfed […]
item.content:encoded:
SURKHET: While the rate of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months has been steadily declining in Nepal in recent years, breastfeeding rates are improving in Karnali Province. Karnali is now among the country’s top-performing provinces on this indicator.

According to the Nepal Demographic and Health Survey, 74% of infants in Karnali are exclusively breastfed for the first six months—18 percentage points higher than the national average of 56%.

The improvement in breastfeeding practices in Karnali was highlighted during an orientation on the protection, promotion and support of breastfeeding organized in Birendranagar by the Karnali Province Health Services Directorate on Wednesday.

Presenting an overview of breastfeeding practices in Nepal, paediatrician Dr Subash Sharma said the national exclusive breastfeeding rate declined from 70% in 2011 to 66% in 2016 and further to 56% in 2022.

Provincial data show that Karnali and Sudurpashchim have the highest exclusive breastfeeding rates at 74% each. Madhesh follows with 65%, Gandaki with 64%, Koshi with 53% and Bagmati with 43%. Similarly, Lumbini has the lowest rate at 36%, according to Sharma.

According to health experts, initiating breastfeeding within one hour of birth and feeding infants only breast milk for the first six months are crucial for a child’s health, nutrition and immune system development. In Nepal, 55% of newborns are breastfed within an hour of birth, while 94% continue to be breastfed up to the age of two.

Speaking at the program, UNICEF Nutrition Officer Sher Singh Dahit said women working in government, non-governmental and private sectors are entitled to at least 98 days of paid maternity leave before or after childbirth. “Legal provisions that require workplaces to facilitate breastfeeding until a child reaches the age of two have helped encourage breastfeeding practices,” he added.

Similarly, Advocate Tulasa Bhandari said the Mother’s Milk Substitutes (Control of Sale and Distribution) Act, 1992 aims to protect and promote breastfeeding by regulating the sale, distribution and advertisement of infant feeding products. “This law helps curb unchecked promotion of breast milk substitutes, ensures product quality, and supports the provision of safe and adequate nutrition for infants,” she added.

Director of the Health Services Directorate Dr Rabin Khadka said breastfeeding remains the most effective means of ensuring infants’ health, nutrition and overall development. “The provincial government has been continuously working to improve maternal and child health through effective implementation of legal provisions, public awareness campaigns and the creation of breastfeeding-friendly environments,” he added.

The data also suggest a link between breastfeeding practices and socioeconomic as well as educational status. Exclusive breastfeeding is more common among low-income families, with a rate of 64%, compared to 44% among high-income households. Similarly, 59% of mothers with no formal education exclusively breastfeed their infants, compared to 53% of mothers who have completed secondary education.

Meanwhile, the use of feeding bottles has been increasing. The practice, which stood at 3% in 1996, rose to 22% in 2022. In Karnali, however, only 11% percent of infants are fed using bottles. This is one of the lowest rates in the country.
